linear-models-s1.title: Sleep and reaction time, with a regression line
linear-models-s1.text: For 14 student volunteers, the regression line for predicting reaction time (milliseconds) from hours of sleep the night before is $\hat{y} = 391.1 - 11.37x$. The students slept from 4.5 to 9.5 hours. (Invented data.)

plot.label: Scatterplot of hours of sleep against reaction time for 14 students with the regression line from about 345 milliseconds at 4 hours down to about 277 at 10 hours

linear-models-s2.title: Used phone prices
linear-models-s2.text: A resale site fits a regression line to 60 listings of one phone model, aged 0 (new, unopened) to 6 years: $\widehat{\text{price}} = 620 - 95(\text{age})$, with price in dollars and age in years. (Invented data.)

table.caption: The regression line
rows: change in predicted price per year of age

items.q: What reaction time does the line predict for a student who slept 6.8 hours?

options: That is only the slope times 6.8. Add it to the intercept with its sign: $391.1 - 77.3$.
That adds the slope term. The slope is negative, so subtract.
That is the intercept, the prediction for 0 hours of sleep.
About 77 milliseconds
About 468 milliseconds
About 314 milliseconds
About 391 milliseconds

items.q: Which is the correct interpretation of the slope?

why.correct: Slope: "for each additional [unit of $x$], the predicted [$y$] increases (decreases) by about $|b|$ [units of $y$]".
options: Right: the slope is the predicted change in $y$ for each one-unit increase in $x$, in context.
That describes the intercept, and 0 hours is far outside the data.
The line predicts reaction time from sleep, not the other way round.
The line gives predictions, not exact changes for each student. Say "predicted".
For each extra hour of sleep, predicted reaction time drops by about 11.4 ms
A student who slept 0 hours is predicted to react in 391 milliseconds
For each millisecond of reaction time, predicted sleep decreases by 11.4 hours
For each additional hour of sleep, reaction time decreases by exactly 11.4 milliseconds

items.q: The line predicts a reaction time of about 243 milliseconds for a student who sleeps 13 hours. How much should this prediction be trusted?

why.correct: Extrapolation: predicting outside the range of $x$ values in the data.
options: Predictions inside the data range are reasonable for typical students. The problem is extrapolating.
Right: no one in the data slept that long, so there is no reason to think the linear trend continues there.
Any $x$ gives a number; that does not make the prediction sensible.
A strong association inside the data says nothing about values far outside it.
Hardly, because predictions do not work for one person
Very little: 13 hours is far outside the data, so it is extrapolation
Fully, because the equation gives a number
Fully, because the association between sleep and reaction time is strong

why.correct: Slope: predicted change in $y$ per one-unit increase in $x$.

change.label: For each
options: For each additional year of age,
For each additional dollar of price,
For a phone that is 1 year old,

why.1: Price is the response; the slope is per unit of the explanatory variable, age.
why.2: That would be a prediction for one age, not the slope.

amount.label: Change
options: the predicted price decreases by about 95 dollars.
the price of each phone drops by exactly 95 dollars.
the predicted price is 95 dollars.

why.1: The line describes predicted values, not exact changes for each phone.
why.2: The slope is a change in price, not a price.

conclude.model: For each additional year of age, the predicted resale price of this phone model decreases by about 95 dollars.

items.q: Interpret the intercept in context. Does it make sense here?

why.correct: Intercept: the predicted $y$ when $x = 0$, worth interpreting only when $x = 0$ is in or near the data.

value.label: Intercept
options: A new phone (age 0) has a predicted price of 620 dollars,
Each phone loses 620 dollars of value,
The average phone in the data costs 620 dollars,

why.1: The intercept is a predicted price, not a loss.
why.2: The intercept is the prediction at age 0, not the average price.

sense.label: Does it make sense?
options: and this makes sense, since new phones (age 0) are in the data.
but this never makes sense, since an intercept is always extrapolation.
and this is the exact price of every new phone.

why.1: An intercept makes sense when $x = 0$ is a reasonable value inside the data, as here.
why.2: The line gives a predicted value; actual prices vary.

conclude.model: When the phone is new (age 0 years), its predicted resale price is 620 dollars. This makes sense because the data include new phones.

items.q: Write the expression for the predicted price of a 3.5-year-old phone, then evaluate it.

mistakes.why: Multiply the slope by the age first, then subtract from the intercept: $620 - 95(3.5)$.
The slope is negative: price falls with age, so subtract.

items.q: What does the line predict for an 8-year-old phone, and what does that show?

why.correct: Predictions far outside the data can be meaningless.
options: Substitute carefully: $620 - 760 = -140$. And the line cannot tell us about ages beyond 6.
Use the age: $620 - 95(8)$.
A negative price is a sign the line does not apply outside the data, not a real prediction.
Right: $620 - 95(8) = -140$. Extrapolation can give nonsense.
$140$ dollars, the value after the phone stops losing value
$525$ dollars, the intercept minus the slope
$-140$ dollars, so the seller would pay the buyer to take it
$-140$, impossible: 8 years is outside the data

items.q: In $\widehat{\text{price}} = 620 - 95(\text{age})$, what does the hat on "price" mean?

options: The hat does not mean a maximum.
The hat marks a prediction for a given age, not one overall average.
The hat marks a predicted value.
Right: $\hat{y}$ is a predicted value; actual prices scatter around it.
It is the highest price in the data
It is the average of the 60 listed prices in the data
It is the price in a different currency
A predicted price, not an actual listed price

items.q: A line for predicting quiz score (points) from study time (hours) has slope 4.2. What are the units of the slope?

options: That flips the ratio. The slope is $y$ units over $x$ units.
Right: a slope is a change in $y$ per unit of $x$.
A slope is a rate: points per hour.
Unlike $r$, a slope carries units of $y$ per unit of $x$.
Hours per point
Points per hour
Points
It has no units, like a correlation

items.q: A regression line has slope 2.5 and passes through the point $(4, 30)$. What is its equation?

why.correct: Substitute the point into $\hat{y} = a + bx$ and solve for $a$.
options: Subtract 10 from 30, do not add it.
That uses the $y$ value as the intercept. Solve $30 = a + 2.5(4)$.
That uses the $x$ value as the intercept.

items.q: For children aged 5 to 12, a line predicts height (cm) from age (years): $\hat{y} = 76 + 6.2x$. Why should the intercept not be interpreted as a newborn's height?

why.correct: Interpret the intercept only when $x = 0$ makes sense in context.
options: Right: interpreting the intercept here would be extrapolation; real newborns are about 50 cm.
An intercept is meaningful when $x = 0$ is inside the data, as for new phones.
The intercept is the prediction at age 0, not an average.
The sign of the slope does not decide whether the intercept makes sense.
Age 0 is outside the data, and growth is not linear from birth
Intercepts are not meaningful in any regression line
76 cm is the average height of the children in the study
The slope is positive, so the intercept should be ignored

items.q: A scatterplot has correlation $r = -0.7$. What is true of the slope of its regression line?

why.correct: Slope and correlation share their sign.
options: Right: the slope and the correlation always have the same sign.
The slope has units and depends on the spreads of $x$ and $y$; it equals $r$ only in special cases.
A negative correlation means $y$ tends to fall as $x$ rises, so the line falls.
A slope of 0 would mean no linear trend, but $r = -0.7$ shows one.
It is negative
It is $-0.7$
It is positive
It is 0

items.q: A line predicts monthly electricity cost (dollars) from home size (square feet): $\hat{y} = 18 + 0.06x$. Two homes differ in size by 500 square feet. How do their predicted costs differ?

why.correct: A change of $\Delta x$ changes $\hat{y}$ by $b\,\Delta x$.
options: Right: $0.06 \times 500 = 30$ dollars.
That adds the intercept. The intercept cancels when comparing two predictions.
That is the difference for 1 square foot.
Multiply the slope by the difference in size; do not add numbers.
By 30 dollars
By 48 dollars
By 0.06 dollars
By 518 dollars

items.q: The phone line predicts 287.50 dollars for a 3.5-year-old phone. One such phone is listed at 340 dollars. Which statement is correct?

why.correct: Predictions are typical values, not exact ones.
options: One phone above the line does not make the line wrong.
Real data do not fall exactly on a line; that is expected.
Right: $\hat{y}$ is a prediction. Actual values scatter above and below the line.
The line predicts; it does not set prices.
The line is wrong, since it missed this phone
The listing is wrong, since it does not match the line
Individual phones vary around the line's typical price
The phone should sell for exactly 287.50 dollars

items.q: A regression line has intercept 50, and its predicted $y$ falls by 3 for each one-unit increase in $x$. Which is its equation?

options: The intercept is the constant term, 50; the slope multiplies $x$.
That swaps the intercept and the slope.
Right: intercept 50, slope $-3$.
A falling line has a negative slope.
